source: Chapter 2 (unit-02) 'Who Am I?', all five lessons before the rework
why: Lessons 1-4 mostly drilled essere forms, which the grammar unit 'Subject pronouns & essere' now teaches and practises. Lesson 5 (spelling) used avere and articles before they're taught. Some items are reused in the new chapter 2; everything is kept whole here.

grammar_tips.title: Your First Real Verb
grammar_tips.explanation: Until now, everything was memorized phrases. Now you learn how Italian verbs actually work. 'Essere' (to be) changes its form depending on who you're talking about. 'Io sono' = I am. 'Tu sei' = you are. This shape-shifting is called conjugation — and it's how Italian works.

grammar_tips.title: Drop the Pronoun
grammar_tips.explanation: In English, 'I am Marco' needs the 'I'. In Italian, 'Sono Marco' is more natural than 'Io sono Marco'. The verb ending already tells you who's speaking. You only add the pronoun for emphasis or contrast: 'IO sono di Roma, TU sei di Milano.'

grammar_tips.title: Mi chiamo — A Chunk for Now
grammar_tips.explanation: 'Mi chiamo' literally means 'I call myself'. It's a reflexive verb, but don't worry about that yet — just memorize it as a chunk meaning 'my name is'. You'll learn how reflexive verbs actually work in a later unit.

grammar_tips.title: The Third Person: è
grammar_tips.explanation: 'È' means both 'he is' and 'she is' — the verb form is the same. 'Lui è Marco' (he is Marco), 'Lei è Sara' (she is Sara). The accent on è is important: without it, 'e' just means 'and'.

grammar_tips.title: lei vs Lei — Same Sound, Different Meaning
grammar_tips.explanation: 'lei' (lowercase) = she. 'Lei' (capitalized) = you (formal). In speech they sound identical — context tells you which one. When a waiter says 'Lei è di Roma?' they're asking about YOU, not some woman named Roma.

grammar_tips.title: Questo è... Questa è... — Pointing at People
grammar_tips.explanation: 'Questo è Marco' = This is Marco. 'Questa è Sara' = This is Sara. 'Questo' for males, 'questa' for females. Don't overthink the pattern — it's just -o for him, -a for her. You'll see this pattern everywhere in Italian.

grammar_tips.title: Three New Pronouns, Three New Forms
grammar_tips.explanation: 'Noi siamo' = we are. 'Voi siete' = you (plural) are. 'Loro sono' = they are. Notice that 'sono' does double duty — it means both 'I am' (io sono) AND 'they are' (loro sono). Context always makes it clear which one.

grammar_tips.title: The Full Essere Table
grammar_tips.explanation: Here's the complete picture: io sono, tu sei, lui/lei è, noi siamo, voi siete, loro sono. Six forms, but 'sono' covers two of them. That leaves just five unique forms to memorize. Not bad for the most important verb in Italian.

grammar_tips.title: Professions with Essere
grammar_tips.explanation: To say what someone does, use essere: 'Sono studente' (I'm a student), 'Lei è dottoressa' (She's a doctor). In Italian you can drop the article ('un/una') with professions — both 'Sono un insegnante' and 'Sono insegnante' work.

grammar_tips.title: Putting It All Together
grammar_tips.explanation: You now know all six forms of essere, how to give your name, say where you're from, and introduce others. This lesson is pure practice — no new grammar. By the end, you should be able to handle a basic Italian introduction without thinking twice.

grammar_tips.title: Formal vs Informal Introductions
grammar_tips.explanation: With friends: 'Ciao, mi chiamo Marco. Sono di Roma.' With a stranger: 'Buongiorno, sono Marco. Sono di Roma.' The content is almost the same — it's the greeting that sets the register. 'Mi chiamo' works in both, but 'Sono + name' feels slightly more formal.

grammar_tips.title: Piacere — Nice to Meet You
grammar_tips.explanation: 'Piacere' means 'nice to meet you' (literally: 'pleasure'). Say it after someone introduces themselves. It works in any register — formal or informal. You can also say 'Piacere mio' (the pleasure is mine) to be extra polite.

grammar_tips.title: L'Alfabeto Italiano
grammar_tips.explanation: Italian has 21 letters in its standard alphabet (no j, k, w, x, y in native words — they only appear in foreign borrowings). Letter names: a, bi, ci, di, e, effe, gi, acca, i, elle, emme, enne, o, pi, qu, erre, esse, ti, u, vu, zeta.

grammar_tips.title: Spelling Your Name
grammar_tips.explanation: 'Come si scrive?' = 'How do you spell it?'. Reply by saying each letter: 'M-A-R-C-O'. Useful on the phone or with new acquaintances.

grammar_tips.title: Doppia — Double Letters
grammar_tips.explanation: Many Italian words have double consonants ('mamma', 'caffè', 'anno'). When spelling, you say 'doppia' (double) before the letter: 'M-A-doppia M-A' for 'mamma'.
